title: Can quantum-mechanical description of physical reality be considered complete?
text:
Abstract
In a complete theory there is an element corresponding to each element of reality. A sufficient condition for the reality of a physical quantity is the possibility of predicting it with certainty, without disturbing the system. In quantum mechanics in the case of two physical quantities described by non-commuting operators, the knowledge of one precludes the knowledge of the other. Then either (1) the description of reality given by the wave function in quantum mechanics is not complete or (2) these two quantities cannot have simultaneous reality. Consideration of the problem of making predictions concerning a system on the basis of measurements made on another system that had previously interacted with it leads to the result that if (1) is false then (2) is also false. One is thus led to conclude that the description of reality as given by a wave function is not complete.

title: Feller-Style Combinatorial Probability in Finite Sample Spaces
text:
2.1 The Shoes/Socks Selection Problem
A classic problem introduced by Feller concerns selecting items from matched pairs.


Problem Statement: Feller’s Sock/Shoe Matching Problem

A closet contains \(N\) distinct pairs of shoes (or socks), giving a total of \(2N\) individual shoes. Suppose \(r\) shoes are drawn at random without replacement, where \(r \le N\).
What is the probability \(P(E_r)\) that among the \(r\) selected shoes, there is no complete matching pair?

To compute \(P(E_r)\), we enumerate the total and favorable outcomes:

Total Sample Space Size (\(\vert{}\Omega\vert{}\)): The number of ways to choose any \(r\) shoes from \(2N\) available shoes without replacement: \[\vert{}\Omega\vert{} = \binom{2N}{r}\]

Favorable Outcomes (\(\vert{}E_r\vert{}\)): To avoid selecting any complete pair:

First choose \(r\) distinct pairs out of the \(N\) available pairs: \(\binom{N}{r}\) ways.
From each of the \(r\) chosen pairs, select exactly \(1\) shoe (either left or right): \(2^1 = 2\) choices per pair, resulting in \(2^r\) ways.

\[\vert{}E_r\vert{} = \binom{N}{r} 2^r\]


Thus, the probability of selecting no matching pairs is:
\[P(E_r) = \frac{\binom{N}{r} 2^r}{\binom{2N}{r}}\]

Algebraic Simplification and Asymptotic Behavior

Expanding the binomial coefficients explicitly:
\[P(E_r) = \frac{\frac{N!}{r!(N-r)!} 2^r}{\frac{(2N)!}{r!(2N-r)!}} = \frac{N! (2N-r)!}{(N-r)! (2N)!} 2^r\]
We rewrite the ratio of factorials as product ratios:
\[P(E_r) = 2^r \prod_{j=0}^{r-1} \frac{N - j}{2N - j} = \prod_{j=0}^{r-1} \frac{2N - 2j}{2N - j} = \prod_{j=0}^{r-1} \left( 1 - \frac{j}{2N - j} \right)\]
When \(N\) is large relative to \(r\), applying the approximation \(1 - x \approx e^{-x}\) yields:
\[P(E_r) \approx \prod_{j=0}^{r-1} \exp\left( -\frac{j}{2N} \right) = \exp\left( -\frac{1}{2N} \sum_{j=0}^{r-1} j \right) = \exp\left( -\frac{r(r-1)}{4N} \right)\]
This expression reveals the classic birthday-problem phenomenon: even for moderate sample sizes \(r \approx \sqrt{N}\), the probability of encountering at least one matching pair becomes substantial.

title: Feller-Style Combinatorial Probability in Finite Sample Spaces

3.1 Multivariate Hypergeometric Distribution
Suppose an urn contains \(N\) total items partitioned into \(C\) mutually exclusive categories with population counts \(N_1, N_2, \dots, N_C\), such that:
\[\sum_{c=1}^C N_c = N\]
A sample of size \(n\) is drawn at random without replacement (SRSWOR). Let \(X_c\) denote the number of items in the sample belonging to category \(c\).


Definition 2.1: Multivariate Hypergeometric Probability Function

The joint probability mass function of \(\mathbf{X} = (X_1, X_2, \dots, X_C)^\T\) is given by: \[P(X_1 = x_1, X_2 = x_2, \dots, X_C = x_C) = \frac{\prod_{c=1}^C \binom{N_c}{x_c}}{\binom{N}{n}}\] defined for non-negative integers \(x_c\) satisfying \(0 \le x_c \le N_c\) and \(\sum_{c=1}^C x_c = n\).

title: Feller-Style Combinatorial Probability in Finite Sample Spaces
section: 3.2 Combinatorial Examples in Poker and Bridge
text:
3.2 Combinatorial Examples in Poker and Bridge

3.2.1 Example 1: Poker Hand Probabilities (Full House)

Poker Example: Probability of a Full House
Consider dealing a \(5\)-card hand (\(n = 5\)) from a standard \(52\)-card deck (\(N = 52\)). The deck contains \(C = 13\) ranks, with \(N_c = 4\) cards per rank.
A Full House consists of \(3\) cards of one rank and \(2\) cards of another rank:
\[P(\text{Full House}) = \frac{\binom{13}{1} \binom{4}{3} \times \binom{12}{1} \binom{4}{2}}{\binom{52}{5}} = \frac{13 \times 4 \times 12 \times 6}{2,598,960} = \frac{3,744}{2,598,960} \approx 0.001441\]


3.2.2 Example 2: Bridge Hand Suit Distributions (4-4-3-2 Shape)
In contract bridge, a player is dealt a \(13\)-card hand (\(n = 13\)) from a standard deck (\(N = 52\)) partitioned into \(C = 4\) suits of \(N_1 = N_2 = N_3 = N_4 = 13\) cards each.

Bridge Example 1: Probability of a 4-4-3-2 Suit Distribution
Calculate the probability of being dealt a hand with \(4\) cards in two suits, \(3\) cards in a third suit, and \(2\) cards in the remaining suit.

Specific Suit Assignment: The probability of holding \(4\) Spades, \(4\) Hearts, \(3\) Diamonds, and \(2\) Clubs is given by the multivariate hypergeometric formula: \[P(\text{Sp}=4, \text{He}=4, \text{Di}=3, \text{Cl}=2) = \frac{\binom{13}{4} \binom{13}{4} \binom{13}{3} \binom{13}{2}}{\binom{52}{13}}\]

Counting Suit Assignments (Permutations vs. Combinations): To find the total number of ways to assign the shape \(\{4, 4, 3, 2\}\) across the \(4\) named suits (Spades, Hearts, Diamonds, Clubs), we can use two equivalent counting perspectives:


Permutation of Suits (Multinomial Coefficient): Viewing this as arranging \(4\) suit slots where two suits receive \(4\) cards, one receives \(3\) cards, and one receives \(2\) cards: \[\frac{4!}{2! \, 1! \, 1!} = \frac{24}{2 \times 1 \times 1} = 12\] Explanation from basic counting: There are \(4! = 24\) total permutations of the \(4\) suits. However, because \(2\) suits have identical card counts (\(4\) cards each), swapping those two suits does not create a distinct distribution shape. We divide by \(2!\) to eliminate this double-counting, while \(1!\) and \(1!\) account for the unique suit lengths (\(3\) and \(2\) cards).

Alternative Combination (“Choosing”) Argument:

Select \(2\) suits out of \(4\) to hold \(4\) cards each: \(\binom{4}{2} = 6\) ways.
From the remaining \(2\) suits, select \(1\) suit to hold \(3\) cards: \(\binom{2}{1} = 2\) ways.
The remaining \(1\) suit automatically holds \(2\) cards: \(\binom{1}{1} = 1\) way.

Multiplying these sequential choices gives: \[\binom{4}{2} \times \binom{2}{1} \times \binom{1}{1} = 6 \times 2 \times 1 = 12 \text{ ways}\]




Combining these gives the total probability of receiving any \(4\text{-}4\text{-}3\text{-}2\) hand: \[P(\text{4-4-3-2 Distribution}) = 12 \times \frac{\binom{13}{4}^2 \binom{13}{3} \binom{13}{2}}{\binom{52}{13}} = 12 \times \frac{(715)^2 \times 286 \times 78}{635,013,559,600} \approx 0.21551\] Thus, \(4\text{-}4\text{-}3\text{-}2\) is the most common hand distribution in contract bridge, occurring in roughly \(21.55\%\) of all deals.


3.2.3 Example 3: Bridge High Honor Cards Configuration

Bridge Example 2: Holding Specific Honors (Aces and Kings)
What is the probability that a \(13\)-card bridge hand contains exactly 2 Aces and exactly 2 Kings?
Partition the \(52\)-card deck into \(C = 3\) mutually exclusive categories:

Category 1: Aces (\(N_1 = 4\))
Category 2: Kings (\(N_2 = 4\))
Category 3: Other cards (\(N_3 = 44\))

We require selecting \(x_1 = 2\) Aces, \(x_2 = 2\) Kings, and \(x_3 = 13 - (2 + 2) = 9\) other cards:
\[P(X_{\text{Ace}} = 2, X_{\text{King}} = 2) = \frac{\binom{4}{2} \binom{4}{2} \binom{44}{9}}{\binom{52}{13}}\]
Evaluating the binomial coefficients:
\[P(X_{\text{Ace}} = 2, X_{\text{King}} = 2) = \frac{6 \times 6 \times 707,234,155}{635,013,559,600} = \frac{25,460,429,580}{635,013,559,600} \approx 0.04009\]
There is approximately a \(4.01\%\) probability of being dealt exactly \(2\) Aces and \(2\) Kings in a bridge hand.

title: Feller-Style Combinatorial Probability in Finite Sample Spaces
text:
4.1 SRSWOR: The Hypergeometric Distribution
When sampling without replacement, successive draws are dependent. The probability mass function of \(X \sim \text{Hypergeometric}(N, M, n)\) is:
\[P(X = k) = \frac{\binom{M}{k} \binom{N-M}{n-k}}{\binom{N}{n}}, \quad \max(0, n - (N-M)) \le k \le \min(n, M)\]
The mean and variance of \(X\) under SRSWOR are:
\[E[X] = n \left(\frac{M}{N}\right) = np\]
\[\text{Var}_{\text{WOR}}(X) = n p (1-p) \left( \frac{N-n}{N-1} \right)\]
The factor \(\frac{N-n}{N-1}\) is the Finite Population Correction (FPC) factor. Because \(\frac{N-n}{N-1} < 1\) for \(n > 1\), sampling without replacement strictly reduces variance compared to sampling with replacement.

title: Feller-Style Combinatorial Probability in Finite Sample Spaces
text:
4.2 SRSWR: The Binomial Distribution
When sampling with replacement, each draw is an independent Bernoulli trial with constant success probability \(p = M/N\). The probability mass function of \(X \sim \text{Binomial}(n, p)\) is:
\[P(X = k) = \binom{n}{k} p^k (1-p)^{n-k}, \quad k \in \{0, 1, \dots, n\}\]
The mean and variance under SRSWR are:
\[E[X] = np\]
\[\text{Var}_{\text{WR}}(X) = n p (1-p)\]

title: Feller-Style Combinatorial Probability in Finite Sample Spaces
text:
7.1 Simple Random Sampling Without Replacement (SRSWOR)
Under SRSWOR, a sample of \(n\) distinct units is chosen at random without replacement from the \(N\) population units. All possible samples of size \(n\) are equally likely.

7.1.1 Derivation 1: Direct Combinatorial Counting (Unordered Samples)


Method 1: Combination Counting

To find \(P(I_i = 1)\) for any fixed unit \(i \in \{1, 2, \dots, N\}\):

Total Number of Possible Samples: The number of ways to select an unordered sample of \(n\) distinct units from \(N\) population units is: \[\binom{N}{n} = \frac{N!}{n!(N-n)!}\]
Favorable Samples Containing Unit \(i\): If unit \(i\) must be present in the sample, its position is fixed. We are free to select the remaining \(n-1\) sample units from the remaining \(N-1\) population units: \[\binom{N-1}{n-1} = \frac{(N-1)!}{(n-1)!(N-n)!}\]
Inclusion Probability: Under equal likelihood, the ratio of favorable samples to total samples gives: \[P(I_i = 1) = \frac{\binom{N-1}{n-1}}{\binom{N}{n}} = \frac{\frac{(N-1)!}{(n-1)!(N-n)!}}{\frac{N!}{n!(N-n)!}} = \frac{(N-1)!}{N!} \cdot \frac{n!}{(n-1)!} = \frac{n}{N}\]


Thus, for every unit \(i = 1, 2, \dots, N\), the inclusion probability in SRSWOR is simply \(\pi_i = \frac{n}{N}\).

7.1.2 Draw-by-Draw Analysis in SRSWOR
It is instructive to distinguish the overall inclusion probability \(\pi_i = P(I_i = 1)\) from the probability that unit \(i\) appears on a specific draw \(k\).
Define the specific draw indicator \(X_{ik}\) for \(i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) and \(k \in \{1, \dots, n\}\) as:
\[X_{ik} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if unit } i \text{ appears in the } k\text{-th draw of the sample} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\]

Specific Draw Probability Theorem (SRSWOR)
The probability that unit \(i\) is selected on the \(k\)-th draw is equal to \(\frac{1}{N}\) for every draw \(k = 1, 2, \dots, n\).


Proof: Telescoping Conditional Product

For unit \(i\) to be selected specifically on draw \(k\), it must not be selected on draws \(1, 2, \dots, k-1\), and then must be selected on draw \(k\).
Applying the sequential probability rule across draws:
\[\begin{aligned}
P(X_{ik} = 1) &= \underbrace{\left(\frac{N-1}{N}\right)}_{\text{Not on draw 1}} \cdot \underbrace{\left(\frac{N-2}{N-1}\right)}_{\text{Not on draw 2}} \cdots \underbrace{\left(\frac{N-k+1}{N-k+2}\right)}_{\text{Not on draw } k-1} \cdot \underbrace{\left(\frac{1}{N-k+1}\right)}_{\text{Selected on draw } k} \cdot \underbrace{\left(\frac{N-k}{N-k}\dots \frac{N-n}{N-n}\right)}_{\text{Subsequent draws}}
\end{aligned}\]
Notice the telescoping cancellation across all intermediate numerators and denominators:
\[P(X_{ik} = 1) = \frac{\cancel{N-1}}{N} \cdot \frac{\cancel{N-2}}{\cancel{N-1}} \cdot \frac{\cancel{N-3}}{\cancel{N-2}} \dots \frac{\cancel{N-k+1}}{\cancel{N-k+2}} \cdot \frac{1}{\cancel{N-k+1}} = \frac{1}{N}\]
Thus, every single draw \(k \in \{1, \dots, n\}\) has an identical probability \(\frac{1}{N}\) of selecting unit \(i\).


7.1.3 Derivation 2: Alternative Inclusion Derivation via Mutually Exclusive Draw Events
We can now re-derive \(P(I_i = 1)\) using the specific draw probabilities \(P(X_{ik} = 1) = \frac{1}{N}\).
In SRSWOR, unit \(i\) can appear at most once in the sample. Therefore, the events \(\{X_{i1} = 1\}, \{X_{i2} = 1\}, \dots, \{X_{in} = 1\}\) are mutually exclusive.
Since unit \(i\) is included in the sample if and only if it is selected on draw 1, OR draw 2, …, OR draw \(n\):
\[\{I_i = 1\} = \bigcup_{k=1}^n \{X_{ik} = 1\}\]
By the finite additivity axiom for mutually exclusive events:
\[P(I_i = 1) = P\left(\bigcup_{k=1}^n \{X_{ik} = 1\}\right) = \sum_{k=1}^n P(X_{ik} = 1) = \sum_{k=1}^n \frac{1}{N} = n \times \frac{1}{N} = \frac{n}{N}\]
This confirms the result obtained from combination counting.

title: Feller-Style Combinatorial Probability in Finite Sample Spaces
text:
7.2 Simple Random Sampling With Replacement (SRSWR)
Under SRSWR, \(n\) draws are conducted sequentially with replacement. On each draw, every unit in the population has an equal probability \(\frac{1}{N}\) of being selected, independently of all other draws.

7.2.1 Derivation 1: Combinatorial Counting via Complement (Ordered Samples)


Method 1: Counting Ordered Sequences


Total Number of Possible Ordered Samples: Because drawing is done with replacement, each of the \(n\) draws has \(N\) possible outcomes, giving a total sample space size of: \[|\Omega_{\text{WR}}| = N^n\]
Samples Excluding Unit \(i\): For unit \(i\) not to appear in the sample, every single one of the \(n\) draws must select one of the other \(N-1\) remaining population units. The number of such ordered sequences is: \[(N-1)^n\]
Non-Inclusion Probability: Under equal likelihood, the probability that unit \(i\) is excluded from the sample is: \[P(I_i = 0) = \frac{(N-1)^n}{N^n} = \left(\frac{N-1}{N}\right)^n = \left(1 - \frac{1}{N}\right)^n\]
Inclusion Probability: By the complement rule, the inclusion probability \(\pi_i = P(I_i = 1)\) under SRSWR is: \[P(I_i = 1) = 1 - P(I_i = 0) = 1 - \left(1 - \frac{1}{N}\right)^n \quad \text{for } i = 1, 2, \dots, N\]



7.2.2 Draw-by-Draw Analysis and Complementary Product in SRSWR
Let \(X_{ik} = 1\) if unit \(i\) is selected on draw \(k\), and \(0\) otherwise. Because each draw is conducted independently with replacement:
\[P(X_{ik} = 1) = \frac{1}{N} \quad \text{and} \quad P(X_{ik} = 0) = 1 - \frac{1}{N} \quad \text{for all } k = 1, 2, \dots, n\]

Derivation 2: Product Rule for Independent Complements
Unit \(i\) is excluded from the sample if and only if it fails to be drawn on draw 1, AND on draw 2, …, AND on draw \(n\):
\[\{I_i = 0\} = \bigcap_{k=1}^n \{X_{ik} = 0\}\]
Because the draws are independent in SRSWR, the joint probability factors into a product:
\[P(I_i = 0) = P\left(\bigcap_{k=1}^n \{X_{ik} = 0\}\right) = \prod_{k=1}^n P(X_{ik} = 0) = \prod_{k=1}^n \left(1 - \frac{1}{N}\right) = \left(1 - \frac{1}{N}\right)^n\]
Applying the complement rule gives:
\[P(I_i = 1) = 1 - \left(1 - \frac{1}{N}\right)^n\]

title: Feller-Style Combinatorial Probability in Finite Sample Spaces
section: 7.3 Comparison: SRSWOR vs. SRSWR Inclusion Probabilities
text:
7.3 Comparison: SRSWOR vs. SRSWR Inclusion Probabilities
Comparing the inclusion probabilities across the two designs:
\[\pi_i^{\text{WOR}} = \frac{n}{N} \qquad \text{vs.} \qquad \pi_i^{\text{WR}} = 1 - \left(1 - \frac{1}{N}\right)^n\]
For sample size \(n = 1\), both probabilities are identical: \(\pi_i^{\text{WOR}} = \pi_i^{\text{WR}} = \frac{1}{N}\).
For \(n \ge 2\) and \(N \ge 2\), we claim that \(\pi_i^{\text{WR}} < \pi_i^{\text{WOR}}\). Proving this is equivalent to showing that:
\[\left(1 - \frac{1}{N}\right)^n > 1 - \frac{n}{N}\]

Formal Proofs of the Strict Inequality


Method 1: Proof via Bernoulli’s Inequality (Direct & Shortest)

Bernoulli’s Inequality: For any real number \(x > -1\) with \(x \neq 0\) and any integer \(n \ge 2\):
\[(1 + x)^n > 1 + nx\]
Setting \(x = -\frac{1}{N}\):

Since population size \(N \ge 2\), we have \(x = -\frac{1}{N} \in [-0.5, 0)\), which satisfies \(x > -1\) and \(x \neq 0\).
Applying Bernoulli’s Inequality yields: \[\left(1 - \frac{1}{N}\right)^n > 1 + n\left(-\frac{1}{N}\right) = 1 - \frac{n}{N}\]

Multiplying both sides by \(-1\) (reversing the inequality direction) and adding \(1\): \[1 - \left(1 - \frac{1}{N}\right)^n < \frac{n}{N} \implies \pi_i^{\text{WR}} < \pi_i^{\text{WOR}} \quad \blacksquare\]





Method 2: Proof via Binomial Expansion Term-Pairing

To prove the inequality directly from the binomial expansion without ignoring alternating signs, expand \((1 - x)^n\) where \(x = \frac{1}{N}\):
\[\left(1 - x\right)^n = 1 - nx + \sum_{k=2}^n (-1)^k \binom{n}{k} x^k\]
We need to show that the remainder series \(R = \sum_{k=2}^n (-1)^k \binom{n}{k} x^k > 0\). Group adjacent terms into pairs \((T_k, T_{k+1})\) starting at \(k=2\) for even \(k\):
\[T_k + T_{k+1} = \binom{n}{k} x^k - \binom{n}{k+1} x^{k+1} = \binom{n}{k} x^k \left( 1 - \frac{n-k}{k+1} x \right)\]
Because \(n \le N\) in valid sampling designs, \(x = \frac{1}{N} \le \frac{1}{n}\). Thus:
\[\frac{n-k}{k+1} x \le \frac{n-k}{(k+1)n} < 1 \implies \left( 1 - \frac{n-k}{k+1} x \right) > 0\]
Since every even term \(T_k\) is strictly greater in magnitude than its following odd term \(T_{k+1}\), every paired sum is strictly positive. If \(n\) is even, the final term \(T_n = x^n > 0\) is also positive. Thus, the total sum of remaining terms is strictly positive (\(R > 0\)), establishing:
\[\left(1 - \frac{1}{N}\right)^n = 1 - \frac{n}{N} + R > 1 - \frac{n}{N} \implies \pi_i^{\text{WR}} < \pi_i^{\text{WOR}} \quad \blacksquare\]



Method 3: Proof via Mathematical Induction on \(n\)


Base Case (\(n = 2\)): \[\left(1 - \frac{1}{N}\right)^2 = 1 - \frac{2}{N} + \frac{1}{N^2} > 1 - \frac{2}{N} \quad \text{since } \frac{1}{N^2} > 0\] The base case holds strictly.
Inductive Hypothesis: Assume \(\left(1 - \frac{1}{N}\right)^k > 1 - \frac{k}{N}\) holds for some integer \(k \ge 2\).
Inductive Step (\(k \to k+1\)): Multiply both sides by \(\left(1 - \frac{1}{N}\right) > 0\): \[\begin{aligned}
\left(1 - \frac{1}{N}\right)^{k+1} &> \left(1 - \frac{k}{N}\right)\left(1 - \frac{1}{N}\right) \\
&= 1 - \frac{k}{N} - \frac{1}{N} + \frac{k}{N^2} \\
&= 1 - \frac{k+1}{N} + \frac{k}{N^2}
\end{aligned}\] Since \(k \ge 2\) and \(N \ge 2\), the term \(\frac{k}{N^2} > 0\). Therefore: \[\left(1 - \frac{1}{N}\right)^{k+1} > 1 - \frac{k+1}{N}\] By induction, the inequality holds for all integers \(n \ge 2\). \(\blacksquare\)



Optional Review: Elementary Proofs of Bernoulli’s Inequality


Theorem: Bernoulli’s Inequality

For any integer \(n \ge 1\) and any real number \(x \ge -1\):
\[(1 + x)^n \ge 1 + nx\]
Furthermore, if \(n \ge 2\) and \(x \neq 0\), the inequality is strict: \((1 + x)^n > 1 + nx\).



Proof 1: By Mathematical Induction (Most General)


Base Case (\(n = 1\)): \[(1 + x)^1 = 1 + 1 \cdot x = 1 + x\] The inequality holds (as an equality). For \(n = 2\) with \(x \neq 0\): \[(1 + x)^2 = 1 + 2x + x^2 > 1 + 2x \quad \text{since } x^2 > 0\]
Inductive Hypothesis: Assume \((1 + x)^k \ge 1 + kx\) holds for some integer \(k \ge 1\).

Inductive Step (\(k \to k+1\)): Since \(x \ge -1\), we know that \((1 + x) \ge 0\). Multiplying both sides of the hypothesis by \((1 + x)\) preserves the inequality: \[\begin{aligned}
(1 + x)^{k+1} &\ge (1 + kx)(1 + x) \\
&= 1 + x + kx + kx^2 \\
&= 1 + (k + 1)x + \underbrace{kx^2}_{\ge 0} \\
&\ge 1 + (k + 1)x
\end{aligned}\]
Since \(k \ge 1\) and \(x^2 \ge 0\), dropping \(kx^2\) yields \((1 + x)^{k+1} \ge 1 + (k+1)x\). If \(x \neq 0\), \(kx^2 > 0\), making the inequality strict. By induction, the statement holds for all \(n \ge 1\). \(\blacksquare\)





Proof 2: By Calculus / Minimization (For \(x > -1\))

Define the differentiable function \(f(x) = (1 + x)^n - (1 + nx)\) on the domain \(x \in (-1, \infty)\) for fixed \(n \ge 2\).

Find Critical Points: Take the first derivative with respect to \(x\): \[f'(x) = n(1 + x)^{n-1} - n = n \left[ (1 + x)^{n-1} - 1 \right]\] Setting \(f'(x) = 0\) yields \((1 + x)^{n-1} = 1 \implies x = 0\).

Determine Sign of Derivative:

For \(-1 < x < 0\): \((1 + x) < 1 \implies (1 + x)^{n-1} < 1 \implies f'(x) < 0\) (function is strictly decreasing).
For \(x > 0\): \((1 + x) > 1 \implies (1 + x)^{n-1} > 1 \implies f'(x) > 0\) (function is strictly increasing).


Conclusion: \(x = 0\) is the unique global minimum of \(f(x)\) on \((-1, \infty)\). Since \(f(0) = (1+0)^n - (1 + 0) = 0\), we have \(f(x) > f(0) = 0\) for all \(x \neq 0\). Thus: \[(1 + x)^n - (1 + nx) > 0 \implies (1 + x)^n > 1 + nx \quad \blacksquare\]




Proof 3: By Binomial Expansion (Direct for \(x \ge 0\))

For \(x \ge 0\) and integer \(n \ge 2\), expand \((1 + x)^n\) directly using the Binomial Theorem:
\[(1 + x)^n = \sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k} x^k = 1 + nx + \binom{n}{2}x^2 + \binom{n}{3}x^3 + \dots + x^n\]
Since \(x \ge 0\), every term \(\binom{n}{k} x^k \ge 0\) for \(k \ge 2\). Truncating the expansion after the first two terms immediately gives:
\[(1 + x)^n = 1 + nx + \underbrace{\sum_{k=2}^n \binom{n}{k} x^k}_{\ge 0} \ge 1 + nx\]
If \(x > 0\), the term \(\binom{n}{2}x^2 > 0\), making the inequality strictly greater. \(\blacksquare\)


Intuitive Summary:
In SRSWR, duplicate draws of the same unit are allowed, which “wastes” sample slots on already-selected items. Consequently, the probability of including any given distinct unit \(i\) in SRSWR is strictly less than in SRSWOR (\(\pi_i^{\text{WR}} < \pi_i^{\text{WOR}}\) for \(n > 1\)). However, as \(N \to \infty\), applying \((1 - 1/N)^n \approx 1 - n/N\) shows that both inclusion probabilities converge to \(\frac{n}{N}\).

text:
1.2 Sample Indicators and Inclusion Probabilities
To formalize design-based randomness, we introduce the sample inclusion indicator for each population unit \(i \in U\):
\[I_i = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if unit } i \text{ is included in the sample } s \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\]
Because \(I_i\) is a Bernoulli random variable under the sampling design:

First-order inclusion probability (\(\pi_i\)): The marginal probability that unit \(i\) is sampled: \[\pi_i = P(I_i = 1) = E(I_i)\]
Second-order (joint) inclusion probability (\(\pi_{ij}\)): The probability that both units \(i\) and \(j\) are sampled: \[\pi_{ij} = P(I_i = 1, I_j = 1) = E(I_i I_j)\]



Fundamental Property of Inclusion Probabilities

Inclusion probabilities are marginal probabilities across population units; thus, \(\sum_{i=1}^N \pi_i \neq 1\). Instead, the sum of inclusion probabilities across all population units equals the expected sample size:
\[\sum_{i=1}^N \pi_i = \sum_{i=1}^N E(I_i) = E\left(\sum_{i=1}^N I_i\right) = E(n) = n\]

title: Horvitz-Thompson Estimation Theory and Applications
text:
2.1 Definition
The Horvitz-Thompson estimator for the population total \(Y = \sum_{i=1}^N Y_i\) weights each observed value \(y_i\) by the inverse of its inclusion probability \(w_i = 1/\pi_i\):
\[\hat{Y}_{HT} = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{y_i}{\pi_i} = \sum_{i=1}^N I_i \frac{Y_i}{\pi_i}\]
The estimator for the population mean \(\bar{Y}\) is simply:
\[\hat{\bar{Y}}_{HT} = \frac{1}{N} \hat{Y}_{HT} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{y_i}{\pi_i}\]
Proof: Unbiasedness of the Horvitz-Thompson Estimator

To prove that \(E(\hat{Y}_{HT}) = Y\) for any probability sampling design with \(\pi_i > 0\):
\[E(\hat{Y}_{HT}) = E\left( \sum_{i=1}^N I_i \frac{Y_i}{\pi_i} \right)\]
By linearity of expectation:
\[E(\hat{Y}_{HT}) = \sum_{i=1}^N E(I_i) \frac{Y_i}{\pi_i}\]
Since \(E(I_i) = \pi_i\):
\[E(\hat{Y}_{HT}) = \sum_{i=1}^N \pi_i \frac{Y_i}{\pi_i} = \sum_{i=1}^N Y_i = Y \quad \blacksquare\]

Derivation: Theoretical Variance of the HT Estimator

To compute \(\text{Var}(\hat{Y}_{HT})\), we evaluate the variance and covariances of the sample indicators \(I_i\):

Variance of indicator \(I_i\): \[\text{Var}(I_i) = E(I_i^2) - (E(I_i))^2 = E(I_i) - \pi_i^2 = \pi_i(1 - \pi_i)\]
Covariance of indicators \(I_i, I_j\) (\(i \neq j\)): \[\text{Cov}(I_i, I_j) = E(I_i I_j) - E(I_i)E(I_j) = \pi_{ij} - \pi_i \pi_j\]

Using the variance formula for a linear combination of random variables:
\[\text{Var}(\hat{Y}_{HT}) = \text{Var}\left( \sum_{i=1}^N I_i \frac{Y_i}{\pi_i} \right) = \sum_{i=1}^N \text{Var}(I_i) \left(\frac{Y_i}{\pi_i}\right)^2 + \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{j \neq i}^N \text{Cov}(I_i, I_j) \left(\frac{Y_i}{\pi_i}\right) \left(\frac{Y_j}{\pi_j}\right)\]
Substituting \(\text{Var}(I_i)\) and \(\text{Cov}(I_i, I_j)\):
\[\text{Var}(\hat{Y}_{HT}) = \sum_{i=1}^N \pi_i(1 - \pi_i) \frac{Y_i^2}{\pi_i^2} + \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{j \neq i}^N (\pi_{ij} - \pi_i \pi_j) \frac{Y_i Y_j}{\pi_i \pi_j}\]
\[\text{Var}(\hat{Y}_{HT}) = \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{1 - \pi_i}{\pi_i} Y_i^2 + \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{j \neq i}^N \frac{\pi_{ij} - \pi_i \pi_j}{\pi_i \pi_j} Y_i Y_j \quad \blacksquare\]

title: Horvitz-Thompson Estimation Theory and Applications
text:
3.1 The Classical Horvitz-Thompson Variance Estimator
Substituting the sample indicator \(I_i I_j / \pi_{ij}\) into the population variance expression yields the plugin sample estimator:
\[\hat{V}_{HT}(\hat{Y}_{HT}) = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{1 - \pi_i}{\pi_i^2} y_i^2 + \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j \neq i}^n \frac{\pi_{ij} - \pi_i \pi_j}{\pi_i \pi_j \pi_{ij}} y_i y_j\]
Provided \(\pi_{ij} > 0\) for all pairs \((i, j)\), \(\hat{V}_{HT}(\hat{Y}_{HT})\) is strictly unbiased for \(\text{Var}(\hat{Y}_{HT})\). However, it has a major practical drawback: it can produce negative variance estimates for certain sample realizations.

title: Horvitz-Thompson Estimation Theory and Applications
text:
3.2 The Sen-Yates-Grundy (SYG) Variance Formulation
For sampling designs with a fixed sample size \(n\) (such as SRSWOR, stratified sampling with fixed \(m_h\), or fixed-size PPS designs), Sen (1953) and Yates & Grundy (1953) showed that the variance can be rewritten into an alternative pairwise difference form.
Derivation: Sen-Yates-Grundy Variance Identity

For any fixed sample size design, \(\sum_{j \neq i}^N \pi_{ij} = (n-1)\pi_i\). Using this identity:
\[\sum_{j \neq i}^N (\pi_{ij} - \pi_i \pi_j) = (n-1)\pi_i - \pi_i (n - \pi_i) = -\pi_i(1 - \pi_i)\]
Substituting \(\pi_i(1 - \pi_i) = -\sum_{j \neq i}^N (\pi_{ij} - \pi_i \pi_j)\) into the theoretical HT variance formula allows us to group terms into squared differences:
\[\text{Var}_{SYG}(\hat{Y}_{HT}) = -\frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{j \neq i}^N (\pi_{ij} - \pi_i \pi_j) \left( \frac{Y_i}{\pi_i} - \frac{Y_j}{\pi_j} \right)^2 \quad \blacksquare\]

The corresponding Sen-Yates-Grundy sample variance estimator is:
\[\hat{V}_{SYG}(\hat{Y}_{HT}) = -\frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j \neq i}^n \frac{\pi_{ij} - \pi_i \pi_j}{\pi_{ij}} \left( \frac{y_i}{\pi_i} - \frac{y_j}{\pi_j} \right)^2\]


Comparison: HT vs. Sen-Yates-Grundy Variance Estimators


Condition for Non-Negativity: The SYG estimator \(\hat{V}_{SYG}\) is guaranteed to be non-negative for every sample realization whenever \(\pi_{ij} \le \pi_i \pi_j\) for all \(i \neq j\). This condition holds for SRSWOR and most well-behaved fixed-size sampling designs.
Stability: \(\hat{V}_{SYG}\) is generally more stable and exhibits lower variance than \(\hat{V}_{HT}\) because it is constructed from weighted pairwise differences \((y_i/\pi_i - y_j/\pi_j)^2\).
Applicability: SYG requires a fixed sample size design (\(n = \text{const}\)). For variable sample size designs, the classical HT variance estimator must be used.

title: Horvitz-Thompson Estimation Theory and Applications
section: 4.1 Design 1: Simple Random Sampling Without Replacement (SRSWOR)
text:
4.1 Design 1: Simple Random Sampling Without Replacement (SRSWOR)

Design Rule: Every sample of size \(n\) from \(N\) has equal probability \(\binom{N}{n}^{-1}\).
Inclusion Probability: \(\pi_i = \frac{\binom{N-1}{n-1}}{\binom{N}{n}} = \frac{n}{N}\).
HT Estimator: \[\hat{Y}_{HT} = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{y_i}{n/N} = \frac{N}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n y_i = N \bar{y}\]

title: Horvitz-Thompson Estimation Theory and Applications
text:
4.2 Design 2: Stratified Random Sampling

Design Rule: Population is divided into \(K\) non-overlapping strata of size \(M_h\) (\(\sum_{h=1}^K M_h = N\)). An SRSWOR of size \(m_h\) is independently drawn from each stratum \(h\).
Inclusion Probability: For unit \(j\) in stratum \(h\), \(\pi_{(h,j)} = \frac{m_h}{M_h}\).
HT Estimator: \[\hat{Y}_{HT} = \sum_{h=1}^K \sum_{j=1}^{m_h} \frac{y_{(h,j)}}{\pi_{(h,j)}} = \sum_{h=1}^K \frac{M_h}{m_h} \sum_{j=1}^{m_h} y_{(h,j)} = \sum_{h=1}^K M_h \bar{y}_h\]
HT Population Mean: \[\hat{\bar{Y}}_{HT} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{h=1}^K M_h \bar{y}_h = \sum_{h=1}^K W_h \bar{y}_h \quad \text{where } W_h = \frac{M_h}{N}\]

title: Horvitz-Thompson Estimation Theory and Applications
text:
4.3 Design 3: Single-Stage Cluster Sampling

Design Rule: Population consists of \(N\) primary clusters, each containing \(M_i\) secondary elements. An SRSWOR of \(n\) clusters is sampled, and all \(M_i\) elements in sampled clusters are measured.
Inclusion Probability: For element \(j\) in cluster \(i\), \(\pi_{(i,j)} = P(\text{Cluster } i \text{ sampled}) = \frac{n}{N}\).
HT Estimator: \[\hat{Y}_{HT} = \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^{M_i} \frac{y_{(i,j)}}{n/N} = \frac{N}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n M_i \bar{y}_i\]

Means:


Per Cluster: \(\hat{\bar{Y}}_{\text{per cluster}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n M_i \bar{y}_i\)


Per Element: \(\hat{\bar{Y}}_{\text{per element}} = \frac{N}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \left(\frac{M_i}{M_{\text{pop}}}\right) \bar{y}_i\), where \(M_{\text{pop}} = \sum_{i=1}^N M_i\).

title: Horvitz-Thompson Estimation Theory and Applications
text:
4.4 Design 4: Two-Stage Sampling

Design Rule: First stage draws \(n\) PSUs out of \(N\) via SRSWOR. Second stage draws an SRSWOR of \(m_i\) SSUs out of \(M_i\) within each selected PSU \(i\).
Inclusion Probability: By independence across stages: \[\pi_{(i,j)} = P(Z_i = 1) \times P(I_{(i,j)} = 1 \mid Z_i = 1) = \left(\frac{n}{N}\right) \times \left(\frac{m_i}{M_i}\right)\]
HT Estimator: \[\hat{Y}_{HT} = \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^{m_i} \frac{y_{(i,j)}}{\left(\frac{n}{N}\right)\left(\frac{m_i}{M_i}\right)} = \frac{N}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n M_i \left( \frac{1}{m_i} \sum_{j=1}^{m_i} y_{(i,j)} \right) = \frac{N}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n M_i \bar{y}_i\]

Proof: Unbiasedness in Two-Stage Sampling via Iterated Expectations

Let \(Z_i \in \{0,1\}\) indicate PSU selection and \(I_{(i,j)} \in \{0,1\}\) indicate SSU selection within PSU \(i\).
First, evaluate the conditional expectation of \(\bar{y}_i\) given \(Z_i\):
\[E(\bar{y}_i \mid Z_i) = E\left( \frac{1}{m_i} \sum_{j=1}^{M_i} I_{(i,j)} Y_{(i,j)} \,\,\Bigg\vert{}\,\, Z_i \right) = \frac{1}{m_i} \sum_{j=1}^{M_i} E(I_{(i,j)} \mid Z_i) Y_{(i,j)}\]
From the conditional probability distribution \(P(I_{(i,j)} = 1 \mid Z_i = 1) = \frac{m_i}{M_i}\) and \(P(I_{(i,j)} = 1 \mid Z_i = 0) = 0\), we have \(E(I_{(i,j)} \mid Z_i) = \frac{m_i}{M_i} Z_i\).
\[E(\bar{y}_i \mid Z_i) = \frac{1}{m_i} \sum_{j=1}^{M_i} \left(\frac{m_i}{M_i} Z_i\right) Y_{(i,j)} = Z_i \bar{Y}_i\]
Now applying the law of iterated expectations \(E(\cdot) = E_Z[E(\cdot \mid Z)]\):
\[E\left( \frac{N}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n M_i \bar{y}_i \right) = E\left( \frac{N}{n} \sum_{i=1}^N Z_i M_i \bar{y}_i \right) = \frac{N}{n} \sum_{i=1}^N M_i E\left[ Z_i E(\bar{y}_i \mid Z_i) \right]\]
Since \(Z_i^2 = Z_i\):
\[E\left( \frac{N}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n M_i \bar{y}_i \right) = \frac{N}{n} \sum_{i=1}^N M_i E(Z_i) \bar{Y}_i = \frac{N}{n} \sum_{i=1}^N M_i \left(\frac{n}{N}\right) \bar{Y}_i = \sum_{i=1}^N M_i \bar{Y}_i = \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{j=1}^{M_i} Y_{(i,j)} \quad \blacksquare\]

title: Horvitz-Thompson Estimation Theory and Applications
section: 4.5 Design 5: Probability Proportional to Size (PPS / \(\pi\)PS) Sampling
text:
4.5 Design 5: Probability Proportional to Size (PPS / \(\pi\)PS) Sampling
When positive auxiliary measure of size \(X_i > 0\) (e.g., hospital bed count, clinic patient volume) is known for all units \(i \in U\), we can design an unequal probability scheme where first-order inclusion probabilities are proportional to \(X_i\):
\[\pi_i = n \frac{X_i}{\sum_{k=1}^N X_k} = n \frac{X_i}{X_{\text{total}}}\]

Efficiency Principle: If the response variable \(Y_i\) is roughly proportional to \(X_i\) (i.e., \(Y_i \approx c X_i\)), then the ratio \(Y_i / \pi_i \approx c X_{\text{total}} / n\) is nearly constant across all units.
Zero Variance Ideal: If \(Y_i = c X_i\) perfectly for all \(i\), then \(\text{Var}(\hat{Y}_{HT}) = 0\). PPS sampling achieves massive variance reduction over equal-probability SRSWOR whenever \(Y\) and \(X\) are strongly correlated.

title: Horvitz-Thompson Estimation Theory and Applications
text:
6.1 The Setup
A circus statistician wants to estimate the total weight \(Y = \sum_{i=1}^{N} Y_i\) of a herd of \(N = 50\) elephants.
The circus owner knows that Elephant 1, named Sambo, is a famous elephant whose weight is known beforehand to be \(Y_1 = 5,000\text{ lbs}\). The statistician decides to sample \(n = 1\) elephant to estimate the herd’s total weight using a design-based approach.
To be helpful, the statistician constructs an unequal probability sampling design:

Sambo (Unit 1): Drawn with probability \(p_1 = \pi_1 = 0.99\).
Other Elephants (Units \(2, \ldots, 50\)): Drawn with equal probability \(p_i = \pi_i = \frac{0.01}{49} \approx 0.000204\) for each \(i \in \{2, \ldots, 50\}\).

Notice that \(\sum_{i=1}^{50} \pi_i = 0.99 + 49 \left(\frac{0.01}{49}\right) = 1.0\), satisfying valid sampling design requirements.

title: Horvitz-Thompson Estimation Theory and Applications
text:
6.2 The Outcomes
When the sample of size \(n = 1\) is drawn, only two realizations are possible under the Horvitz-Thompson estimator \(\hat{Y}_{HT} = \frac{y_i}{\pi_i}\):

6.2.1 Realization A: Sambo is Selected (Probability = 0.99)
Sambo is weighed, yielding \(y_1 = 5,000\text{ lbs}\). The HT estimate for the total herd weight is:
\[\hat{Y}_{HT} = \frac{5,000}{0.99} \approx 5,050.51\text{ lbs}\]

Interpretation: Since Sambo weighs \(5,000\text{ lbs}\), estimating the total herd weight at \(5,050.51\text{ lbs}\) implies that the remaining 49 elephants weigh a combined \(50.51\text{ lbs}\) (about \(1\text{ lb}\) each).


6.2.2 Realization B: Any Other Elephant is Selected (Probability = 0.01)
Suppose Elephant 2 is selected with an actual weight of \(Y_2 = 3,000\text{ lbs}\). The HT estimate for the total herd weight is:
\[\hat{Y}_{HT} = \frac{3,000}{\left(\frac{0.01}{49}\right)} = 3,000 \times 4,900 = 14,700,000\text{ lbs}\]

Interpretation: Estimating total weight at \(14.7\text{ million lbs}\) implies that each elephant in the herd weighs an average of \(294,000\text{ lbs}\).

title: Horvitz-Thompson Estimation Theory and Applications
text:
6.3 The Theoretical Paradox
Mathematical Proof: Unbiasedness of Basu’s HT Estimator

Despite producing ridiculous numbers in every single realization, the estimator remains strictly unbiased under sample space repetition:
\[E(\hat{Y}_{HT}) = \sum_{i=1}^{50} \pi_i \left( \frac{Y_i}{\pi_i} \right)\]
\[E(\hat{Y}_{HT}) = (0.99)\left(\frac{Y_1}{0.99}\right) + \sum_{i=2}^{50} \left(\frac{0.01}{49}\right)\left(\frac{Y_i}{\frac{0.01}{49}}\right)\]
\[E(\hat{Y}_{HT}) = Y_1 + \sum_{i=2}^{50} Y_i = \sum_{i=1}^{50} Y_i = Y \quad \blacksquare\]

While \(E(\hat{Y}_{HT}) = Y\) holds, the sampling variance \(\text{Var}(\hat{Y}_{HT})\) is astronomically large. In practice, a statistician gets only one sample realization, and in Basu’s setup, 100% of realized outcomes are contextually impossible.


Core Takeaways for Survey Design


Optimal Design Weighting: The HT estimator performs exceptionally well when inclusion probabilities are proportional to size (\(\pi_i \propto Y_i\)). It fails when inverse inclusion weights (\(1/\pi_i\)) are extreme and uncorrelated with the size of \(Y_i\).
Design Unbiasedness vs. Practical Utility: Unbiasedness is an average property across hypothetical repeated samples. An unbiased estimator with extreme conditional variance can be useless for real-world decision-making.
Incorporate Auxiliary Information: If known baseline quantities exist (such as Sambo’s weight \(Y_1\)), use model-assisted, difference, or calibration estimators rather than forcing unequal design weights into an unassisted HT formula: \[\hat{Y}_{\text{diff}} = Y_1 + \hat{Y}_{\text{remaining}}\]

title: Probability Sampling in Finite Populations
section: 1.1 Finite Sample Spaces and Elementary Events
text:
1.1 Finite Sample Spaces and Elementary Events
Let \(\Omega\) be a non-empty, finite set of all possible outcomes of a random experiment. We refer to \(\Omega\) as the sample space.


Definition 1.1: Finite Sample Space and Elementary Events

A sample space \(\Omega\) is finite if it contains a finite number of elements \(M = \vert{}\Omega\vert{} < \infty\), such that: \[\Omega = \{\omega_1, \omega_2, \dots, \omega_M\}\] Each individual outcome \(\omega_m \in \Omega\) is called an elementary outcome (or outcome). The singleton sets \(\{\omega_m\}\) are called elementary events.

In finite population sampling, the random experiment consists of selecting a subset of units from a finite target population \(U\). The outcomes \(\omega_m\) correspond to specific realized samples.

title: Probability Sampling in Finite Populations
text:
1.2 The Event Space \(\mathcal{F}\)

An event \(A\) is a subset of the sample space, \(A \subseteq \Omega\). The collection of all observable events forms the event space (or \(\sigma\)-algebra) \(\mathcal{F}\).

Key Structural Property: Because \(\Omega\) is finite, the natural choice for the event space \(\mathcal{F}\) is the complete power set of \(\Omega\), denoted by \(\mathcal{P}(\Omega)\). The power set consists of all \(2^M\) possible subsets of \(\Omega\): \[\mathcal{F} = \mathcal{P}(\Omega) = \{ A : A \subseteq \Omega \}, \quad \vert{}\mathcal{F}\vert{} = 2^{\vert{}\Omega\vert{}}\]

The algebraic operations on events directly parallel standard set operations:


Union (\(A \cup B\)): Event that \(A\) or \(B\) (or both) occur.

Intersection (\(A \cap B\)): Event that both \(A\) and \(B\) occur.

Complement (\(A^c\) or \(\Omega \setminus A\)): Event that \(A\) does not occur.

Disjoint/Mutually Exclusive Events: \(A \cap B = \emptyset\).

title: Probability Sampling in Finite Populations
text:
2.1 Probability Assigned via Elementary Outcomes
Because \(\Omega = \{\omega_1, \dots, \omega_M\}\) is finite, any event \(A \in \mathcal{F}\) can be represented uniquely as the disjoint union of its constituent elementary events: \[A = \bigcup_{\omega_m \in A} \{\omega_m\}\]
Applying Axiom 3 (Finite Additivity), the probability of any event \(A\) is fully determined by the probabilities assigned to the elementary outcomes:
\[P(A) = \sum_{\omega_m \in A} P(\{\omega_m\})\]
Let \(p_m = P(\{\omega_m\})\) denote the probability mass assigned to elementary event \(\{\omega_m\}\). The probability measure \(P\) is completely specified by the vector \(\mathbf{p} = (p_1, \dots, p_M)^\T\) subject to:

\(p_m \ge 0 \quad \forall m \in \{1, \dots, M\}\)
\(\sum_{m=1}^M p_m = 1\)


Proof: Fundamental Consequences of Kolmogorov’s Axioms

From Kolmogorov’s Axioms, we derive several immediate properties for any \(A, B \in \mathcal{F}\):

Empty Set Probability: \(P(\emptyset) = 0\). \[\Omega = \Omega \cup \emptyset \implies P(\Omega) = P(\Omega) + P(\emptyset) \implies 1 = 1 + P(\emptyset) \implies P(\emptyset) = 0\]
Complement Rule: \(P(A^c) = 1 - P(A)\). \[A \cup A^c = \Omega \text{ with } A \cap A^c = \emptyset \implies P(A) + P(A^c) = P(\Omega) = 1 \implies P(A^c) = 1 - P(A)\]

Inclusion-Exclusion Principle: \(P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)\). Decompose \(A \cup B\) into the disjoint union of \(A\) and \(B \setminus A\): \[A \cup B = A \cup (B \setminus A)\]
Applying Axiom 3 (Finite Additivity) gives: \[P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B \setminus A)\]
To find an expression for \(P(B \setminus A)\), decompose \(B\) into the disjoint union of \(B \cap A\) and \(B \setminus A\): \[B = (B \cap A) \cup (B \setminus A)\]
Applying Axiom 3 to \(B\) yields: \[P(B) = P(B \cap A) + P(B \setminus A)\]
Rearranging terms gives: \[P(B \setminus A) = P(B) - P(A \cap B)\]
Substituting this expression for \(P(B \setminus A)\) back into \(P(A \cup B)\) completes the proof: \[P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)\]

title: Probability Sampling in Finite Populations
section: 3.1 Target Population and Sample Space of Samples
text:
3.1 Target Population and Sample Space of Samples
Let \(U = \{1, 2, \dots, N\}\) denote a fixed, finite target population of \(N\) known, labeled units.


Definition 1.3: Sampling Design as a Probability Measure

A sample \(s\) is a subset of the population, \(s \subseteq U\). Let \(\mathcal{S} \subseteq \mathcal{P}(U)\) denote the set of all candidate samples allowed under a given protocol. The sample space of the sampling experiment is \(\Omega = \mathcal{S}\).
A sampling design \(p(s)\) is a probability density function with respect to the counting measure on \(\mathcal{S}\), defining a probability measure \(P\) on \((\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{S}))\): \[p(s) = P(S = s) = P(\{s\})\] satisfying: \[p(s) \ge 0 \quad \forall s \in \mathcal{S}, \quad \text{and} \quad \sum_{s \in \mathcal{S}} p(s) = 1\]

title: Probability Sampling in Finite Populations
text:
3.2 Unit Inclusion as Events
In design-based survey sampling, the randomness resides entirely in the selection mechanism \(S \sim p(s)\), not in the population characteristics \(\mathbf{y} = (y_1, \dots, y_N)^\T\).
Let \(A_i\) be the event that population unit \(i \in U\) is selected into the random sample \(S\): \[A_i = \{s \in \mathcal{S} : i \in s\}\]
Using our axiomatic definition, the probability of event \(A_i\) defines the first-order inclusion probability \(\pi_i\):
\[\pi_i = P(A_i) = P(i \in S) = \sum_{s \in \mathcal{S} : i \in s} p(s)\]
Similarly, the event that both unit \(i\) and unit \(j\) are selected is \(A_i \cap A_j = \{s \in \mathcal{S} : i, j \in s\}\), giving the second-order inclusion probability \(\pi_{ij}\):
\[\pi_{ij} = P(A_i \cap A_j) = P(i, j \in S) = \sum_{s \in \mathcal{S} : i, j \in s} p(s)\]

Proof: Sum of First-Order Inclusion Probabilities for Fixed-Size Designs

Let \(S\) be a random sample under a fixed-size sampling design where \(\vert{}s\vert{} = n\) for all \(s \in \mathcal{S}\) with \(p(s) > 0\). Consider the sum of first-order inclusion probabilities over all \(N\) population units:
\[\sum_{i=1}^N \pi_i = \sum_{i=1}^N \left( \sum_{s \in \mathcal{S} : i \in s} p(s) \right)\]
To make the set-restricted summation explicit, we introduce an indicator function \(\mathbb{I}(i \in s)\), which equals \(1\) if unit \(i\) is contained in sample \(s\) and \(0\) otherwise:
\[\sum_{i=1}^N \pi_i = \sum_{i=1}^N \left( \sum_{s \in \mathcal{S}} p(s) \mathbb{I}(i \in s) \right)\]
Because both index sets (\(i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) and \(s \in \mathcal{S}\)) are finite, we can interchange the order of summation—swapping the outer sum over units \(i\) with the inner sum over candidate samples \(s\):
\[\sum_{i=1}^N \pi_i = \sum_{s \in \mathcal{S}} \left( \sum_{i=1}^N p(s) \mathbb{I}(i \in s) \right)\]
Since \(p(s)\) depends only on the sample \(s\) and does not change with unit index \(i\), we factor \(p(s)\) out of the inner sum over \(i\):
\[\sum_{i=1}^N \pi_i = \sum_{s \in \mathcal{S}} p(s) \left( \sum_{i=1}^N \mathbb{I}(i \in s) \right)\]
Notice that the inner sum \(\sum_{i=1}^N \mathbb{I}(i \in s) = \sum_{i \in s} 1 = \vert{}s\vert{}\) counts the total number of units in sample \(s\). Under a fixed-size sampling design, every sample with \(p(s) > 0\) contains exactly \(\vert{}s\vert{} = n\) units:
\[\sum_{i=1}^N \pi_i = \sum_{s \in \mathcal{S}} p(s) \cdot n = n \sum_{s \in \mathcal{S}} p(s)\]
Finally, since \(p(s)\) is a normalized probability distribution over \(\mathcal{S}\), we have \(\sum_{s \in \mathcal{S}} p(s) = 1\):
\[\sum_{i=1}^N \pi_i = n \cdot 1 = n\]

title: Probability Sampling in Finite Populations
text:
4.1 Conceptual Loop-Based Approach
The program below mirrors the theoretical definition of event summation directly. It sequentially evaluates set membership by explicitly checking, for each unit \(i\) (and each pair \(i, j\)), which candidate samples in \(\mathcal{S}\) contain that unit, and sums the corresponding design probabilities \(p(s)\).
What this program demonstrates:


Direct Translation of Set Summation: It evaluates the exact finite-sum formulas \(\pi_i = \sum_{s: i \in s} p(s)\) and \(\pi_{ij} = \sum_{s: \{i,j\} \subseteq s} p(s)\) using nested loops and set containment functions (i %in% s).

Pedagogical Value: It explicitly exposes how individual sample events are identified and aggregated, helping students visualize the mechanics of inclusion probabilities.

Computational Inefficiency: It illustrates why scalar loops scale poorly in scientific R code. For an \(N\)-unit population and sample space of size \(M\), computing \(\boldsymbol{\Pi}\) requires \(O(N^2 \cdot M)\) individual set evaluations.


# Target Population Parameters
U <- 1:5
N <- length(U)
n <- 3

# Enumerate sample space S (SRSWOR)
S_list <- combn(U, n, simplify = FALSE)
M <- length(S_list)
p_s <- rep(1 / M, M)

# 1. First-order inclusion probabilities (pi_i) via explicit looping
pi_loop <- numeric(N)
for (i in 1:N) {
  event_A_i <- sapply(S_list, function(s) i %in% s)
  pi_loop[i] <- sum(p_s[event_A_i])
}

# 2. Second-order inclusion probabilities (pi_ij) via double looping
pi_matrix_loop <- matrix(0, nrow = N, ncol = N)
for (i in 1:N) {
  for (j in 1:N) {
    if (i == j) {
      pi_matrix_loop[i, j] <- pi_loop[i]
    } else {
      event_A_ij <- sapply(S_list, function(s) (i %in% s) && (j %in% s))
      pi_matrix_loop[i, j] <- sum(p_s[event_A_ij])
    }
  }
}

title: Probability Sampling in Finite Populations
text:
4.2 Idiomatic R: Vectorized Matrix-Algebra Approach
In modern statistical computing, design-based survey calculations are naturally formulated in terms of matrix operations. We encapsulate the entire sample space structure inside an \(M \times N\) binary sample indicator matrix \(\mathbf{Z}\), where entry \(Z_{m, i}\) indicates whether unit \(i\) is selected in sample \(s_m\):
\[Z_{m, i} = \mathbb{I}(i \in s_m) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } i \in s_m \\ 0 & \text{if } i \notin s_m \end{cases}\]
Using linear algebra, our theoretical quantities become direct matrix-vector products:

First-Order Inclusion Probabilities: The \(N \times 1\) vector \(\boldsymbol{\pi} = (\pi_1, \dots, \pi_N)^\T\) is obtained by weighting the indicator columns of \(\mathbf{Z}\) by the design probability vector \(\mathbf{p} = (p(s_1), \dots, p(s_M))^\T\): \[\boldsymbol{\pi} = \mathbf{Z}^\T \mathbf{p}\] In R, this matrix product \(X^\T Y\) is computed via crossprod(Z, p_s) without allocating explicit transposes in memory.
Second-Order Inclusion Probability Matrix: The \(N \times N\) matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Pi} = (\pi_{ij})\) contains diagonal entries \(\pi_{ii} = \pi_i\) and off-diagonal entries \(\pi_{ij} = \sum_{m=1}^M Z_{m,i} Z_{m,j} p(s_m)\). In matrix notation: \[\boldsymbol{\Pi} = \mathbf{Z}^\T \text{diag}(\mathbf{p}) \mathbf{Z}\] In R, scaling the rows of \(\mathbf{Z}\) by \(\mathbf{p}\) is achieved via element-wise multiplication p_s * Z (due to column-major matrix storage), allowing us to compute \(\boldsymbol{\Pi}\) via crossprod(Z, p_s * Z) in a single BLAS-optimized call.

What this program demonstrates:


Full Vectorization: It eliminates all explicit loops by operating directly on the matrix representation \(\mathbf{Z}\) of the sample space.

BLAS Optimization: It highlights best-practice numerical routines in R—specifically using crossprod() instead of t() to compute matrix transpositions inline, significantly reducing memory allocations and computing time.

Equivalence & Precision: It confirms that the vectorized approach produces identical numerical results to the scalar loop implementation while scaling efficiently to large sample spaces.


# 1. Direct Matrix Construction (M x N) without explicit t() or loops
Z <- matrix(
  as.numeric(sapply(S_list, function(s) U %in% s)), 
  nrow = M, 
  ncol = N, 
  byrow = TRUE
)
colnames(Z) <- paste0("Unit_", U)
rownames(Z) <- paste0("Sample_", 1:M)

cat("Sample Indicator Matrix Z (M x N):\n")

names(pi_vec) <- paste0("Unit_", 1:N)

# 3. Second-order inclusion matrix: Pi = Z^T %*% diag(p) %*% Z via crossprod()

title: Statistical innovation in science
text:
Overview
The advent of Geographical Information Systems and related technologies have led to a burgeoning of spatial databases in a diverse set of disciplines. Statisticians and spatial analysts often encounter large to massive spatial and spatial-temporal data sets that are incomplete, involve layers of complex dependencies and demand accurate assessment of uncertainty. Professor Banerjee has undertaken several such projects throughout his career in substantive scientific fields such as ecology, forestry, climate and the environment, and public health.

title: Mechanistic systems
text:
Overview
Machine learning and high performance computing have unfurled conundrums surrounding the role of mechanistic modeling in scientific inference. Mechanistic systems refer to models built from scientific principles and laws that help understand complex mechanisms posited to be generating observational data. While machine learning algorithms often seek to circumvent the complex mechanisms through the use of large-scale data sets, mechanistic models attempt to directly relate the data to the laws of basic science. These two modeling paradigms often tend to operate exclusive to each other. Dr. Banerjee has developed approaches for integrating these two apparently antagonistic paradigms into a single comprehensive inferential framework. Building upon developments in Bayesian inferential frameworks for spatial-temporal mechanistic models, Dr. Banerjee has proposed stochastic dynamical systems engendering full probabilistic uncertainty quantification for environmental processes.

title: Multivariate spatial processes
text:
Overview
Multivariate spatial processes refer to collections of spatial or spatial-temporal processes, where each process captures spatial dependence while also being associated with the other processes in the collection. Building valid multivariate processes and multivariate spatial probability laws is a crucial exercise in the analysis of environmental and public health data where different spatially-oriented variables of interest are associated among themselves in addition to being spatially dependent. Multivariate processes also arise in constructing spatially varying regression models, where the slopes in the regression model are spatial processes designed to capture associations in the way they impact the outcome or response over space and time. Statistical models for capturing multivariate spatial dependencies must also overcome complications arising from spatial misalignment and change of support problems, which refer to settings when not all of the variables of interest have been measured over the same set of spatial locations. Professor Banerjee has published an array of articles on developing rich and flexible yet computationally practicable methods for analyzing complex multivariate dependencies in spatial data arising in environmental sciences and public health research.

title: Spatial ‘BIG DATA’
text:
Overview
Spatial process models for analyzing geostatistical data entail computations that become prohibitive as the number of spatial locations become large. Dr. Banerjee has led pioneering contributions in model-based solutions for spatial “BIG DATA” analysis. These include the development and implementation of classes of low-rank spatial process models known as “predictive processes” that achieve dimension-reduction by projecting the original process on an optimal lower-dimensional subspace. Another, more recent, line of research led by Dr. Banerjee develop sparsity-inducing spatial processes known as “Nearest-Neighbor Gaussian processes” (NNGP) that achieve scalabilty by exploiting sparsity in models without discarding spatial information. Finally, Dr. Banerjee has also explored “meta-kriging”, which refers to dividing and conquering massive spatial data sets by analyzing subsets of the data and subsequently pooling the analyses to draw inference for the entire data. These approaches have attracted significant attention among statisticians and practitioners and are widely deployed to deliver inference for massive spatial databases without compensating for richness of modeling.

R Packages

spBayes: Univariate and Multivariate Spatio-temporal Modeling


spBayes fits univariate and multivariate models with Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC). Core functions include:

spLM: univariate Gaussian regression with spatial random effects
spMvLM: multivariate Gaussian regression with spatial random effects
spMisalignLM: multivariate Gaussian regression with spatial random effects for misaligned data
spGLM: univariate Logistic and Poisson regression with spatial random effects
spMvGLM: multivariate Logistic and Poisson regression with spatial random effects
spMisalignGLM: multivariate Logistic and Poisson regression with spatial random effects for misaligned data
spDynLM: univariate Gaussian regression with dynamic space-time random effects





For the core functions, a predictive process model can be specified for large data sets. Also adaptive MCMC is available for those parameters that cannot be updated using Gibbs. The stable version is available on CRAN.


spNNGP: Spatial Regression Models for Large Datasets using Nearest Neighbor Gaussian Processes


spNNGP fits Gaussian univariate Bayesian spatial regression models for massive datasets using “Nearest Neighbor Gaussian Processes (NNGP)”. Core functions include:

CHM: Canopy Height Model from NASA Goddard’s LiDAR Hyperspectral and Thermal (G-LiHT)
spConjNNGP: Function for fitting univariate Bayesian conjugate spatial regression models
spNNGP: Function for fitting univariate Bayesian spatial regression models
spPredict: Function for prediction at new locations using spNNGP models





The stable version is available on CRAN.


spStack: Bayesian Geostatistics Using Predictive Stacking


Fast Bayesian inference for Gaussian and non-Gaussian geospatial models without using Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms. This R package is written in C++ with calls to FORTRAN routines for optimized linear algebra operations. Core functions include:

spLMstack: spatial linear model using Bayesian predictive stacking
spGLMstack: spatial GLM using Bayesian predictive stacking
stvcGLMstack: spatial-temporal GLM using Bayesian predictive stacking
recoverGLMscale: Recover posterior samples of scale parameters in spatial-temporal GLMs
posteriorPredict: Prediction of latent process at new spatial or temporal locations





The stable version is available on CRAN.


MBA: Multilevel B-spline Approximation


MBA generates surfaces interpolated from scattered data using Multilevel B-Splines. The most recent version is available on CRAN.






B2Z: Bayesian Two-Zone Model


This package fits the Bayesian two-zone models. The most recent version is available on CRAN.

Statpack.zip
Statpack.zip  is a zip file containing the following files:

lapack.cpp: a C++ file containing several matrix algebra functions, including basic matrix and vector operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication, kronecker products), matrix inversion, solving linear systems, determinants, log-determinants, matrix decompositions (Cholesky, LU, QR and SVD), eigen-values and eigen-vectors etc. Only C++ classes have been used (not templates) to make this more accessible (for example C programmers can easily port these functions). The header file containing the class definitions is lapack.h.

A makefile format for creating a static library, StatPack.a is also included.

title: Software

Java Programs

Statpack.jar

Statpack.jar  is a Java Archive file containing the JAMA (JAvaMAtrix) package from NIST (I have added a kronecker method for kronecker products and a symmetrize method that helps in stabilizing symmetric matrices for Cholesky decompositions). Also included is a Distribution package with classes for random number generation, and some useful functions for spatial modelling. Just add StatPack.jar to your CLASSPATH and you should be able to access the methods.



JaLAJni

JaLAJni: These are JAVA packages providing Java interfaces for numerical linear algebra using the LAPACK and BLAS libraries. This contains two different versions: JaLAJni and JaLAJniLite. Both of them serve as a Java interface for LAPACK and BLAS. The main difference is that JaLAJni calls an intermediate C interface - cblas and lapacke - which requires previous installation. So if you want to use JaLAJni, you have to install cblas and lapacke first (detailed installation instructions are available from the website). JaLAJniLite is a simplified version which requires no installation of any libraries other than LAPACK and BLAS that can be installed in Linux/Windows/MacOS either as precompiled binaries or built from source using Fortran compilers (such as gfortran).



JAMAJni

JAMAJni: These are JAVA packages providing Java interfaces for numerical linear algebra using the matrix classes provided by JAMA. However, unlike JAMA, JAMAJni uses LAPACK and BLAS libraries for matrix computations. The JAMAJni github page contains two different versions: JAMAJni and JAMAJniLite. Both of them serve as a Java interface for LAPACK and BLAS. The main difference is that JAMAJni calls an intermediate C interface - cblas and lapacke - which requires previous installation. So if you want to use JAMAJni, you have to install cblas and lapacke first (detailed installation instructions are available from the website). JAMAJniLite is a simplified version which requires no installation of any libraries other than LAPACK and BLAS that can be installed in Linux/Windows/MacOS either as precompiled binaries or built from source using Fortran compilers (such as gfortran).

LinearModel.zip  contains some simple linear model examples that are fitted using MCMC. They include Gibbs samplers, component-wise Metropolis (in subdirectory Metropolis) and joint Metropolis (in two different Java styles, uner Metropolis2 and Metropolis3). These do not really need MCMC, but can prove useful for someone starting to hard-code MCMC. Uses the statpack.jarfile.

Spatial data analysis for massive data sets with complex dependencies often require specialized computational algorithms in conjunction with scalable models. Spatial variation in survival patterns often reveal underlying lurking factors, which, in turn, assist researchers and data science professionals in their decision making process to identify regions requiring attention. title: Disease mapping
text:
Overview
Regional aggregates of health outcomes over delineated administrative units (e.g., states, counties, and zip codes), or areal units, are widely used by epidemiologists to map mortality or incidence rates and capture geographic variation. Spatial dependence in such models are usually captured using graphical probability distributions such as Markov random fields that model the spatial effects conditionally given the effects of neighboring regions. Professor Banerjee has explored diverse aspects of such models and their inferential performance. He has developed novel classes of multivariate conditional auto-regression (MCAR) models and models building upon directed acyclic graphs (DAGAR models). He has also published original developments on spatial boundary analysis or areal wombling to identify neighboring regions with significant health oriented spatial disparities.

title: Spatial gradients
text:
Overview
Stochastic process models are widely employed for analyzing spatiotemporal datasets in various scientific disciplines including, but not limited to, environmental monitoring, ecological systems, forestry, hydrology, meteorology, and public health. After inferring on a spatiotemporal process for a given dataset, inferential interest may turn to estimating rates of change, or gradients, over space and time. Dr. Banerjee has developed fully model-based inference on spatiotemporal gradients under continuous space, continuous time settings. Dr. Banerjee’s contribution has been to offer, within a flexible spatiotemporal process model setting, a framework to estimate arbitrary directional gradients over space at any given time-point, temporal derivatives at any given spatial location and, finally, mixed spatiotemporal gradients that reflect rapid change in spatial gradients over time and vice-versa.

title: Sudipto Banerjee
text:
Dr. Sudipto Banerjee currently serves as Senior Associate Dean in the Fielding School of Public Health. He is a Professor in the UCLA Department of Biostatistics with a joint appointment in the UCLA Department of Statistics and Data Science and an affiliate appointment in the UCLA Institute of the Environment and Sustainability. He served as the Chair of the Department of Biostatistics at UCLA from 2014 through 2023. He served as the elected President of the International Society for Bayesian Analysis in 2022.
His research interests include Bayesian hierarchical modeling and statistical machine learnin methods for complex data systems involving massive datasets (“BIG DATA”); environmental processes and their impact on public health; spatial data science; spatial epidemiology; stochastic process models; statistical learning from physical and mechanistic systems; survey sampling and survival analysis. His theoretical and methodological contributions in statistics are available in the form of several scholarly publications in peer-reviewed journals in statistics, biostatistics and health sciences; an authoritative textbook on spatial statistics; a textbook on linear algebra for statisticians; an edited comprehensive handbook on spatial epidemiology; and two committee reports for the National Research Council of the National Academies. He has served as Principal Investigator of over 14 major federally funded research projects from NIH and NSF primarily devoted to the advancement of statistical and machine learning methods for space-time processes and their substantive impact in data-driven scientific discoveries.

title: Probabilistic Expectations in Finite Populations
text:
1.1 Finite Population Parameters
Let \(U = \{1, 2, \ldots, N\}\) denote a finite target population of \(N\) known units. Associated with each unit \(i \in U\) is a fixed population characteristic \(Y_i\).


Definition 1.1: Finite Population Parameters

We define the following key population parameters:

Population Mean: \[\bar{Y} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N Y_i\]
Population Variance (Sample-Adjusted / Unbiased Version): \[S^2 = \frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{i=1}^N (Y_i - \bar{Y})^2 = \frac{1}{N-1} \left\{\sum_{i=1}^N Y_i^2 - N\bar{Y}^2\right\}\]
Population Variance (Pop. Definition Version): \[\sigma^2 = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N (Y_i - \bar{Y})^2 = \frac{1}{N} \left\{\sum_{i=1}^N Y_i^2 - N\bar{Y}^2\right\}\]
Proportionality Relationship: \[\sigma^2 = \frac{N-1}{N} S^2\]

title: Probabilistic Expectations in Finite Populations
text:
1.2 Sample Statistics
Suppose a sample of fixed size \(n\) is drawn from \(U\), where \(n \le N\) is known.


Definition 1.2: Sample Quantities

Let \(\{y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_n\}\) denote the observed values in the sample. We define:

Sample Mean: \[\bar{y} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n y_i\]
Sample Variance: \[s^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \bar{y})^2 = \frac{1}{n-1} \left\{\sum_{i=1}^n y_i^2 - n\bar{y}^2\right\}\]
Sampling Fraction: \[f = \frac{n}{N}\]

title: Probabilistic Expectations in Finite Populations
section: 2.1 Finite Population Expectation and Design Unbiasedness
text:
2.1 Finite Population Expectation and Design Unbiasedness

Core Design-Based Expectation Principle:
Let \(R = \{r_1, r_2, \dots, r_M\}\) denote the complete collection of all candidate samples allowed under a given sampling design, where \(M = |\mathcal{S}|\). Let \(t(r)\) be any sample statistic (e.g., sample mean \(\bar{y}_r\) or sample variance \(s^2_r\)) computed from sample \(r \in R\).
The design expectation of \(t(r)\) is defined as the sum over all possible samples weighted by their design selection probabilities \(P(r)\): \[\text{E}[t] = \sum_{r \in R} t(r) P(r)\]
A sample statistic \(\hat{\theta}\) is said to be a design-unbiased estimator of a population parameter \(\theta\) if: \[\text{E}[\hat{\theta}] = \theta\]

title: Probabilistic Expectations in Finite Populations
section: 2.2 The Fundamental Theorem: Average of Sample Means Equals Population Mean
text:
2.2 The Fundamental Theorem: Average of Sample Means Equals Population Mean
Under Simple Random Sampling Without Replacement (SRSWOR), each of the \(M = \binom{N}{n}\) distinct samples \(r \in R\) has equal selection probability \(P(r) = 1/\binom{N}{n}\).
The foundation of finite population design inference rests on showing that if we compute the sample mean \(\bar{y}_r\) for every possible sample \(r \in R\) and average them together, the result equals the true population mean \(\bar{Y}\).
\[\text{E}(\bar{y}) = \frac{1}{\binom{N}{n}} \sum_{r \in R} \bar{y}_r = \bar{Y}\]

Proof: Elementary Averaging over All Possible Samples

Let \(R\) be the set of all \(M = \binom{N}{n}\) possible samples of size \(n\) from population \(U = \{1, \dots, N\}\). For any sample \(r \in R\), the sample mean is: \[\bar{y}_r = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i \in r} Y_i\]
Taking the design expectation yields: \[\text{E}(\bar{y}) = \sum_{r \in R} \bar{y}_r P(r) = \frac{1}{\binom{N}{n}} \sum_{r \in R} \left( \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i \in r} Y_i \right) = \frac{1}{n \binom{N}{n}} \sum_{r \in R} \sum_{i \in r} Y_i\]
To evaluate the double sum \(\sum_{r \in R} \sum_{i \in r} Y_i\), consider how many times a specific population unit \(i \in U\) appears across all \(M\) samples in \(R\).

If unit \(i\) is fixed in the sample, the remaining \(n-1\) slots must be chosen from the remaining \(N-1\) population units.
Thus, each unit \(i\) appears in exactly \(\binom{N-1}{n-1}\) distinct samples.

Interchanging the order of summation gives: \[\sum_{r \in R} \sum_{i \in r} Y_i = \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{r \ni i} Y_i = \sum_{i=1}^N \binom{N-1}{n-1} Y_i = \binom{N-1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^N Y_i\]
Substituting this result back into the expectation formula: \[\text{E}(\bar{y}) = \frac{1}{n \binom{N}{n}} \left( \binom{N-1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^N Y_i \right) = \left( \frac{\binom{N-1}{n-1}}{n \binom{N}{n}} \right) \sum_{i=1}^N Y_i\]
Simplifying the ratio of binomial coefficients: \[\frac{\binom{N-1}{n-1}}{\binom{N}{n}} = \frac{\frac{(N-1)!}{(n-1)!(N-n)!}}{\frac{N!}{n!(N-n)!}} = \frac{(N-1)! n!(N-n)!}{N! (n-1)!(N-n)!} = \frac{n}{N}\]
Therefore: \[\text{E}(\bar{y}) = \left( \frac{n}{N} \cdot \frac{1}{n} \right) \sum_{i=1}^N Y_i = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N Y_i = \bar{Y}\]
This completes the proof.

title: Probabilistic Expectations in Finite Populations
section: 3.1 Definition and Properties of Inclusion Indicators
text:
3.1 Definition and Properties of Inclusion Indicators
Define the random variable \(I_i\) for each unit \(i \in \{1, 2, \dots, N\}\) in the population:
\[I_i = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if unit } i \text{ is selected in the sample} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\]
Using inclusion indicators, the sample mean is expressed as a linear combination of population parameters:
\[\bar{y} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^N I_i Y_i\]
Note that in this formulation, \(Y_i\) is fixed and \(I_i\) is the only random variable.


Lemma 3.1: Moments and Covariances of Inclusion Indicators under SRSWOR

For SRSWOR of fixed size \(n\) from population size \(N\):

First Moment / Expectation: \[\text{E}(I_i) = P(I_i = 1) = \frac{\binom{N-1}{n-1}}{\binom{N}{n}} = \frac{n}{N} = f\]
Second Moment (Joint Inclusion Probability): \[\text{E}(I_i^2) = \text{E}(I_i) = \frac{n}{N}\] For \(i \neq j\): \[\text{E}(I_i I_j) = P(I_i = 1, I_j = 1) = \frac{\binom{N-2}{n-2}}{\binom{N}{n}} = \frac{n(n-1)}{N(N-1)}\]
Variance: \[\text{Var}(I_i) = \text{E}(I_i^2) - [\text{E}(I_i)]^2 = \frac{n}{N}\left(1 - \frac{n}{N}\right) = \frac{n(N-n)}{N^2}\]
Covariance (\(i \neq j\)): \[\text{Cov}(I_i, I_j) = \text{E}(I_i I_j) - \text{E}(I_i)\text{E}(I_j) = \frac{n(n-1)}{N(N-1)} - \frac{n^2}{N^2} = -\frac{n(N-n)}{N^2(N-1)}\]



Proof: Unbiasedness of Sample Mean \(\text{E}(\bar{y}) = \bar{Y}\) via Indicators

Using linearity of expectation:
\[\text{E}(\bar{y}) = \text{E}\left( \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^N I_i Y_i \right) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^N \text{E}(I_i) Y_i\]
Substitute \(\text{E}(I_i) = \frac{n}{N}\):
\[\text{E}(\bar{y}) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^N \left( \frac{n}{N} \right) Y_i = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N Y_i = \bar{Y}\]


Proof: Variance of Sample Mean \(\text{Var}(\bar{y}) = \frac{1-f}{n} S^2\) via Indicators

Apply the linear expansion formula for the variance of a sum:
\[\text{Var}(\bar{y}) = \text{Var}\left( \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^N I_i Y_i \right) = \frac{1}{n^2} \left\{ \sum_{i=1}^N Y_i^2 \text{Var}(I_i) + \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{j \neq i}^N Y_i Y_j \text{Cov}(I_i, I_j) \right\}\]
Substitute \(\text{Var}(I_i) = \frac{n(N-n)}{N^2}\) and \(\text{Cov}(I_i, I_j) = -\frac{n(N-n)}{N^2(N-1)}\):
\[\text{Var}(\bar{y}) = \frac{1}{n^2} \left\{ \frac{n(N-n)}{N^2} \sum_{i=1}^N Y_i^2 - \frac{n(N-n)}{N^2(N-1)} \sum_{i=1}^N Y_i \sum_{j \neq i}^N Y_j \right\}\]
Factor out \(\frac{n(N-n)}{N^2}\):
\[\text{Var}(\bar{y}) = \frac{N-n}{n N^2} \left\{ \sum_{i=1}^N Y_i^2 - \frac{1}{N-1} \sum_{i=1}^N Y_i (N\bar{Y} - Y_i) \right\}\]
Expand the term inside the brackets:
\[\sum_{i=1}^N Y_i (N\bar{Y} - Y_i) = N\bar{Y} \sum_{i=1}^N Y_i - \sum_{i=1}^N Y_i^2 = N^2\bar{Y}^2 - \sum_{i=1}^N Y_i^2\]
Substituting this back gives:
\[\sum_{i=1}^N Y_i^2 - \frac{1}{N-1} \left( N^2\bar{Y}^2 - \sum_{i=1}^N Y_i^2 \right) = \left( 1 + \frac{1}{N-1} \right) \sum_{i=1}^N Y_i^2 - \frac{N^2}{N-1}\bar{Y}^2 = \frac{N}{N-1} \left( \sum_{i=1}^N Y_i^2 - N\bar{Y}^2 \right)\]
Recalling \(S^2 = \frac{1}{N-1} \left( \sum_{i=1}^N Y_i^2 - N\bar{Y}^2 \right)\), the expression inside the braces simplifies to \(N S^2\). Therefore:
\[\text{Var}(\bar{y}) = \frac{N-n}{n N^2} \left( N S^2 \right) = \frac{N-n}{n N} S^2 = \frac{1 - f}{n} S^2\]


Proof: Unbiasedness of Sample Variance \(\text{E}(s^2) = S^2\) via Indicators

We write \((n-1)s^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n y_i^2 - n\bar{y}^2 = \sum_{i=1}^N I_i Y_i^2 - n\bar{y}^2\). Taking expectations:
\[\text{E}((n-1)s^2) = \text{E}\left( \sum_{i=1}^N I_i Y_i^2 \right) - n \text{E}(\bar{y}^2) = \sum_{i=1}^N \text{E}(I_i) Y_i^2 - n \left\{ \text{Var}(\bar{y}) + [\text{E}(\bar{y})]^2 \right\}\]
Substitute \(\text{E}(I_i) = \frac{n}{N}\), \(\text{Var}(\bar{y}) = \frac{1-f}{n}S^2\), and \(\text{E}(\bar{y}) = \bar{Y}\):
\[\text{E}((n-1)s^2) = \frac{n}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N Y_i^2 - n \left\{ \frac{1-f}{n} S^2 + \bar{Y}^2 \right\} = \frac{n}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N Y_i^2 - (1-f)S^2 - n\bar{Y}^2\]
Group terms involving the population values:
\[\text{E}((n-1)s^2) = n \left\{ \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N Y_i^2 - \bar{Y}^2 \right\} - (1-f)S^2\]
Notice that \(\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N Y_i^2 - \bar{Y}^2 = \sigma^2 = \frac{N-1}{N} S^2\):
\[\text{E}((n-1)s^2) = n \left( \frac{N-1}{N} S^2 \right) - \left( \frac{N-n}{N} \right) S^2 = \left( \frac{nN - n - N + n}{N} \right) S^2 = \left( \frac{N(n-1)}{N} \right) S^2 = (n-1) S^2\]
Dividing both sides by \(n-1\) yields:
\[\text{E}(s^2) = S^2\]

section: 2.1 Major US Health Surveys and Data Systems
text:
2.1 Major US Health Surveys and Data Systems
Health data scientists routinely analyze large-scale national surveys. Four primary systems illustrate different sampling methodologies and objectives:


National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES):

Structure: Continuous multi-stage probability sample of the non-institutionalized US civilian population.
Unique Feature: Combines household interviews with standardized physical examinations and laboratory tests in Mobile Examination Centers (MECs).



Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS):

Structure: World’s largest continuously conducted health survey, administered by state health departments with CDC support.
Unique Feature: Random-digit-dialed (RDD) landline and cellular telephone survey measuring behavioral risk factors (e.g., smoking, physical activity, alcohol consumption).



National Health Interview Survey (NHIS):

Structure: Cross-sectional household interview survey using complex multi-stage cluster sampling.
Unique Feature: Primary source of national data on healthcare access, chronic conditions, and disability.



US Decennial Census & American Community Survey (ACS):

Structure: The Decennial Census provides complete population counts (\(N\)), while the ACS provides continuous rolling sample estimates of demographic and socio-economic characteristics.
Unique Feature: Supplies the population denominators (\(P\)) required to calculate disease rates, incidence, and mortality across demographic subgroups and geographic boundaries.

title: Survey Data, Censuses, and Age Standardization in Health Sciences
section: 3.1 The Danger of Crude Rate Comparisons: Simpson’s Paradox
text:
3.1 The Danger of Crude Rate Comparisons: Simpson’s Paradox
Directly comparing crude mortality rates across different populations (e.g., two counties, states, or countries) can lead to profoundly misleading conclusions when the populations differ in underlying demographic structures—most notably, age distribution.
Because overall mortality risk increases dramatically with age, a population with a large proportion of elderly residents (e.g., Florida) will naturally exhibit a higher crude mortality rate than a population with a younger demographic profile (e.g., Utah), even if the younger population actually experiences higher mortality rates within every single age bracket.
This phenomenon is a classical manifestation of confounding by age (or Simpson’s Paradox). To make meaningful comparisons, we must adjust for age differences using age standardization.

title: Survey Data, Censuses, and Age Standardization in Health Sciences
section: 3.2 A Concrete Numerical Illustration of Simpson’s Paradox
text:
3.2 A Concrete Numerical Illustration of Simpson’s Paradox
To see Simpson’s Paradox in action, consider two communities with equal total populations of \(N = 100,000\):

County A: An older retiree community where \(80\%\) of the population is \(\ge 65\).
County B: A younger college town where \(80\%\) of the population is \(< 65\).

Suppose County B experiences higher mortality rates than County A in every single age bracket:

Among young residents (\(<65\)): County B’s rate is \(1.5\) per \(1,000\) vs. County A’s \(1.0\) per \(1,000\).
Among older residents (\(\ge 65\)): County B’s rate is \(25.0\) per \(1,000\) vs. County A’s \(20.0\) per \(1,000\).


3.2.1 Data Table and Numerical Setup

library(knitr)

# Construct 2-Stratum Simpson's Paradox Dataset
simpson_df <- data.frame(
  Age_Group = c("Young (<65)", "Old (>=65)"),
  Pop_A = c(20000, 80000),      # County A: 80% Old
  Deaths_A = c(20, 1600),       # Rates: 1.0 per 1k (Young), 20.0 per 1k (Old)
  Pop_B = c(80000, 20000),      # County B: 80% Young
  Deaths_B = c(120, 500)        # Rates: 1.5 per 1k (Young), 25.0 per 1k (Old)
)

# Compute Within-Stratum Age-Specific Rates per 1,000
simpson_df$Rate_A <- (simpson_df$Deaths_A / simpson_df$Pop_A) * 1000
simpson_df$Rate_B <- (simpson_df$Deaths_B / simpson_df$Pop_B) * 1000

# Display Data Table

3.2.2 Hand Calculations: Stratum Rates vs. Overall Crude Rates
To see how the numbers in Table 1 aggregate into overall rates:


Age-Specific Stratum Rates (\(r_h = \frac{D_h}{P_h} \times 1,000\)):


Young (\(<65\)):

County A: \(\frac{20}{20,000} \times 1,000 = 1.00\text{ per } 1,000\)

County B: \(\frac{120}{80,000} \times 1,000 = 1.50\text{ per } 1,000\) (Higher mortality in B)




Old (\(\ge 65\)):

Overall Crude Mortality Rates (\(\text{CMR} = \sum v_h r_h\)):

County A (80% Elderly Population Weight): \[\text{CMR}_A = (0.20 \times 1.00) + (0.80 \times 20.00) = 0.20 + 16.00 = 16.20\text{ per } 1,000\]
County B (80% Young Population Weight): \[\text{CMR}_B = (0.80 \times 1.50) + (0.20 \times 25.00) = 1.20 + 5.00 = 6.20\text{ per } 1,000\]



Even though County B experiences higher mortality rates in every age bracket (\(1.50 > 1.00\) and \(25.00 > 20.00\)), County A’s unadjusted crude rate is nearly 2.6 times higher (\(16.20\) vs. \(6.20\)) simply because \(80\%\) of its population sits in the high-risk elderly stratum.

3.2.3 Graphical Illustration

# Compute Overall Crude Rates per 1,000
crude_A <- (sum(simpson_df$Deaths_A) / sum(simpson_df$Pop_A)) * 1000
crude_B <- (sum(simpson_df$Deaths_B) / sum(simpson_df$Pop_B)) * 1000

        ylab = "Mortality Rate (per 1,000)", main = "Stratum-Specific Rates (Unconfounded)",
        legend.text = TRUE, args.legend = list(x = "topleft", bg = "white"),
        ylim = c(0, 30))

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))


Why Does the Paradox Occur?
The crude mortality rate is a weighted average of stratum rates: \(\text{CMR} = \sum v_h r_h\), where \(v_h = P_h / P\) is the proportion of the population in age stratum \(h\).

County A places \(80\%\) of its weight on the high-risk “Old” stratum (\(r_{\text{old}} = 20.0\)), pulling its crude rate up to \(16.20\) per \(1,000\).
County B places \(80\%\) of its weight on the low-risk “Young” stratum (\(r_{\text{young}} = 1.5\)), pulling its crude rate down to \(6.20\) per \(1,000\).

The unadjusted crude rate reflects the demographic composition of the population rather than its underlying healthcare quality or biological risk.

title: Survey Data, Censuses, and Age Standardization in Health Sciences
text:
4.1 Direct Age Standardization
Direct standardization applies the observed age-specific rates \(r_h\) of a study population to an external standard reference population (e.g., the US 2000 Standard Population).


Formula: Direct Age-Standardized Mortality Rate (ASMR)

Let \(P_h^{\text{std}}\) denote the population size of stratum \(h\) in the standard reference population, and let \(P^{\text{std}} = \sum_{h=1}^H P_h^{\text{std}}\).
The Standard Population Weight for stratum \(h\) is: \[w_h = \frac{P_h^{\text{std}}}{P^{\text{std}}} \quad \text{such that} \quad \sum_{h=1}^H w_h = 1\]
The Direct Age-Standardized Mortality Rate (ASMR) is: \[\text{ASMR} = \sum_{h=1}^H w_h r_h = \sum_{h=1}^H w_h \left(\frac{D_h}{P_h}\right)\]

By applying identical weights \(w_h\) to different study populations, differences in crude rates caused by age structure are completely eliminated.

Conceptual Connection: Age Standardization as Stratified Weighted Estimation


Looking Ahead to Stratified Random Sampling

Notice the exact mathematical form of the Direct Standardized Rate:
\[\text{ASMR} = \sum_{h=1}^H w_h r_h\]
This expression is formally identical to a stratified domain estimator:

The population is partitioned into \(H\) distinct strata defined by age groups.
Within each stratum \(h\), an age-specific rate \(r_h\) is computed.
The overall summary statistic is constructed as a linear combination of stratum-specific estimates weighted by standardized stratum proportions \(w_h\).

Later in this course, when we formalize Stratified Random Sampling, post-stratification, and Horvitz-Thompson estimation, you will recognize that age-standardization is simply an early epidemiological instance of stratified weight adjustment!

section: 4.2 Indirect Age Standardization and the Standardized Mortality Ratio (SMR)
text:
4.2 Indirect Age Standardization and the Standardized Mortality Ratio (SMR)
When stratum-specific death counts \(D_h\) in a small study population are unstable or unavailable, but total deaths \(D_{\text{obs}}\) and age-specific population counts \(P_h\) are known, indirect standardization is used.
Indirect standardization applies reference age-specific mortality rates \(r_h^{\text{std}}\) from a large baseline population (e.g., national rates) to the age structure of the local study population.


Formula: Standardized Mortality Ratio (SMR)


Expected Deaths (\(E\)): The number of deaths expected in the study population if it experienced the reference rates \(r_h^{\text{std}}\): \[E = \sum_{h=1}^H P_h r_h^{\text{std}}\]
Standardized Mortality Ratio (SMR): \[\text{SMR} = \frac{D_{\text{obs}}}{E} = \frac{\sum_{h=1}^H D_h}{\sum_{h=1}^H P_h r_h^{\text{std}}}\]
Indirect Age-Standardized Mortality Rate: \[\text{Indirect ASMR} = \text{SMR} \times \text{CMR}_{\text{std}}\]



Interpretation: An \(\text{SMR} > 1.0\) indicates that the study population experienced more deaths than expected given its age structure, while an \(\text{SMR} < 1.0\) indicates fewer deaths than expected.

5.3 Computing Indirect Standardization and SMR in R
